title: Site Reliability Engineering: SLOs, Error Budgets and Incidents
subtitle: Run services by the numbers: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, burn-rate alerts, toil and on-call, incident response and postmortems, capacity, safe releases and chaos experiments.
outcomes: Define SLIs from user journeys and set SLOs with targets, windows and a documented rationale
Calculate error budgets and burn rates, write an error budget policy and design multiwindow burn-rate alerts
Measure toil and on-call load, and automate operational tasks so that they're idempotent, safe and tested
Run an incident with clear roles and communication, build a UTC timeline and write a blameless postmortem
Plan capacity with headroom, gate canary releases statistically and run chaos experiments with abort conditions
prerequisites: Python and the command line at the level of Python Scripting and Linux for DevOps; pandas basics help. Observability with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry is a good companion for the monitoring side, and CI/CD and Automated Testing for releases. You need Python 3.10 or later with pandas, numpy, pytest, fastapi, uvicorn and httpx.
description:
Reliability isn't an accident or a heroic effort; it's a set of numbers and practices a team agrees and keeps. This course teaches site reliability engineering through one checkout service and its month of traffic. You'll choose SLIs and set SLOs from real measurements, turn them into error budgets, write the policy for when the budget runs out, and replay the month through alerting rules to see why multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts page quickly for real problems and stay quiet otherwise. You'll measure a team's toil and on-call load, and build automation that's safe by default, idempotent and tested.

Then you'll handle what goes wrong: run an incident with clear roles, rebuild its timeline in UTC from logs, alerts and chat, measure what it cost in budget, and write a blameless postmortem. The last module plans capacity with queueing maths and headroom, judges canary releases with a statistical test, and runs a chaos experiment on two local services with a hypothesis and abort conditions. Every lab was run, and its checks quote the real output. Observability with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry implements the alerts in PromQL, and Incident Response Fundamentals covers the extra steps that security incidents need.

modules.title: SLIs and SLOs: defining reliability
modules.summary: Reliability as users experience it: why 100% is the wrong target, how to choose service level indicators, and how to set objectives worth keeping.

lessons.title: Reliability as a feature, and why 100% is wrong
objectives: Explain what site reliability engineering is and how it balances reliability with change
Calculate the downtime an availability target allows
key_points: Site reliability engineering (SRE), which began at Google, applies software engineering to operations: reliability is a feature that's specified, measured and engineered like any other, by people who also write code.

Every extra nine costs more and is worth less: users can't tell 99.99% from 100% through their own networks and devices, while the redundancy, engineering and slower releases needed to get there are real costs.
Downtime per window is (1 − target) × window: 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes in 30 days (40.3 in 28), 99.95% allows 21.6 minutes and 99.99% only 4.3, far too little for anyone to respond to by hand.

A service that needs several dependencies in series can be no more available than their product: three at 99.9% each leave at most about 99.7% before its own failures, unless it degrades gracefully when one of them fails.

The target balances two goods: the reliability users need and the speed of change the business needs. Setting it explicitly turns arguments between development and operations into a shared, measurable decision.

lessons.title: Choosing service level indicators
objectives: Write an SLI as a ratio of good events to valid events
Choose where and how to measure an SLI
key_points: A service level indicator (SLI) is the proportion of valid events that were good, between 0 and 100%: for example, successful checkout requests divided by all checkout requests over a window.

Choose SLIs from what users do: availability and latency for request-driven services, freshness and correctness for data pipelines, durability for storage. Each important user journey, such as search or checkout, gets a few SLIs, not dozens.

Define good and valid precisely, and write it down: is a 4xx the client's mistake or the service's, does a 429 from the service's own rate limiter count against it, are health checks and probes excluded? A 5xx is almost always bad.

Measure latency as a threshold SLI, the share of requests faster than, say, 300 ms, rather than an average, which hides the slow tail. With histogram metrics, put a bucket boundary exactly at the threshold.
Measure as close to users as you can: load balancer logs see failures servers never record, client telemetry also sees the network, and synthetic probes cover quiet periods; each has blind spots.

Request-based SLIs weight every request equally, so a night-time outage at low traffic costs little; time-based SLIs count good minutes, which weighs quiet and busy hours alike but is noisy when traffic is low.

lessons.title: Setting service level objectives
objectives: Set an SLO with a target, a window and an owner
Distinguish an SLO from an SLA and review SLOs over time
key_points: A service level objective (SLO) is a target for an SLI over a window: 99.9% of checkout requests succeed, over a rolling 28 days. A rolling window reflects users' recent experience; a calendar month resets the count on the first of the month.
A 28-day window always holds four of each weekday, so weekly traffic patterns don't make one window's SLI look different from the next.

Base the target on what users need and what the service achieves now: an SLO far above current performance is broken from day one, and one far below it invites decay. Several thresholds can apply at once, such as 90% within 100 ms and 99% within 1 s.
A service level agreement (SLA) is a contract with consequences, such as service credits, so it's set looser than the internal SLO, which then warns the team before the SLA is at risk.
Write an SLO document: each SLI's exact definition and query, the targets and window, the rationale, the owner and a review date. Revisit it, often quarterly at first, as you learn what users notice.

files.content:
"""Generate 28 days of per-minute traffic for the course's checkout service, with five incidents in it.
Columns: minute (UTC), requests, errors_5xx, errors_4xx, and latency buckets: requests answered within
100 ms, 300 ms and 1 s (cumulative, like Prometheus histogram buckets). Fixed seed: everyone gets the same file."""
import pathlib

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
minutes = pd.date_range("2026-06-01", periods=28 * 1440, freq="min", tz="UTC")
hour = minutes.hour + minutes.minute / 60
daily = 0.55 + 0.45 * np.cos((hour - 14) / 24 * 2 * np.pi)        # busiest at 14:00 UTC
weekly = np.where(minutes.dayofweek >= 5, 0.6, 1.0)                  # quieter at weekends
requests = rng.poisson(320 * daily * weekly)

err = np.full(len(minutes), 0.0003)                                  # background 5xx ratio
fast, ok, slow = np.full(len(minutes), 0.80), np.full(len(minutes), 0.992), np.full(len(minutes), 0.999)
incidents = [  # (name, start, minutes, error ratio or None, share within 300 ms or None)
    ("bad deploy", "2026-06-04 14:10", 35, 0.40, None),
    ("night dependency errors", "2026-06-11 02:00", 180, 0.015, None),
    ("slow memory leak", "2026-06-17 10:00", 20 * 60, 0.004, None),
    ("cache misconfiguration", "2026-06-23 09:30", 60, None, 0.80),
    ("network blip", "2026-06-25 20:00", 3, 1.0, None),
]
for _, start, length, e, within_300 in incidents:
    sel = (minutes >= pd.Timestamp(start, tz="UTC")) & (minutes < pd.Timestamp(start, tz="UTC") + pd.Timedelta(minutes=length))
    if e is not None:
        err[sel] = e
    if within_300 is not None:
        fast[sel], ok[sel] = 0.30, within_300

e5 = rng.binomial(requests, err)
answered = requests - e5
e4 = rng.binomial(answered, 0.02)
le_100ms = rng.binomial(requests, fast)
le_300ms = le_100ms + rng.binomial(requests - le_100ms, (ok - fast) / (1 - fast))
le_1s = le_300ms + rng.binomial(requests - le_300ms, (slow - ok) / (1 - ok))

df = pd.DataFrame({"minute": minutes.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ"), "requests": requests, "errors_5xx": e5,
                   "errors_4xx": e4, "le_100ms": le_100ms, "le_300ms": le_300ms, "le_1s": le_1s})
pathlib.Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
df.to_csv("data/traffic.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame(incidents, columns=["name", "start", "minutes", "error_ratio", "within_300ms"]).to_csv(
    "data/incidents.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote data/traffic.csv: {len(df)} minutes, {df.requests.sum():,} requests, {df.errors_5xx.sum():,} 5xx")

"""Module 1 lab: measure the checkout service's SLIs from per-minute traffic and compare them with SLOs."""
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/traffic.csv", parse_dates=["minute"])
total, bad = df.requests.sum(), df.errors_5xx.sum()

# Availability: a request is good unless the service failed it (5xx). 4xx responses are the client's
# mistakes, so they count as valid and good here; that's a decision to write down in the SLO document.
availability = 1 - bad / total
# Latency: the share of all requests answered within 300 ms (the le_300ms bucket boundary must equal it).
latency = df.le_300ms.sum() / total
print(f"28 days: {total:,} requests, {bad:,} failed")
print(f"availability SLI {availability:.4%}   latency SLI (within 300 ms) {latency:.4%}")
for target in (0.99, 0.995, 0.999, 0.9995):
    print(f"  availability SLO {target:.2%}: {'met' if availability >= target else 'missed'}"
          f"   latency SLO {target:.2%}: {'met' if latency >= target else 'missed'}")

daily = df.groupby(df.minute.dt.date)[["requests", "errors_5xx", "le_300ms"]].sum()
daily["availability"] = 1 - daily.errors_5xx / daily.requests
daily["latency"] = daily.le_300ms / daily.requests
print("worst days for availability:")
print(daily.nsmallest(3, "availability")[["requests", "errors_5xx", "availability"]].to_string(
    formatters={"availability": "{:.3%}".format}))

# The same month as a time-based SLI: a minute is good when under 1% of its requests failed.
bad_minute = df.errors_5xx / df.requests > 0.01
in_incident = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
for _, inc in pd.read_csv("data/incidents.csv").iterrows():
    start = pd.Timestamp(inc.start, tz="UTC")
    in_incident |= (df.minute >= start) & (df.minute < start + pd.Timedelta(minutes=inc.minutes))
print(f"time-based availability: {1 - bad_minute.mean():.4%} ({bad_minute.sum()} bad minutes of {len(df)}, "
      f"{(bad_minute & ~in_incident).sum()} of them outside the incidents)")
night = df.minute.dt.hour < 6
print(f"share of requests between 00:00 and 06:00 UTC: {df.requests[night].sum() / total:.1%}")

hints: The scripts need pandas 2.0 or later; check with python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)".
Leaving 4xx responses out of the valid events, instead of counting them as good, changes the SLI slightly. Either is defensible: choose, write it down and keep it consistent.
Missing 99.9% this month doesn't make it the wrong target: one bad deploy did most of the damage. Decide what users need, then let the error budget policy in module 2 handle months like this.

modules.title: Error budgets and alerting on burn rate
modules.summary: Turn an SLO into an error budget, agree what happens when it runs out, and page on how fast it's burning, with the maths behind multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts.

lessons.title: Error budget maths
objectives: Calculate an error budget in events and in time
Calculate burn rates and how long a budget will last
key_points: The error budget is 1 − SLO: with 99.9% over 28 days, 0.1% of the window's valid events may fail. At the lab's 6.28 million requests that's about 6,283 failed requests, or 40.3 minutes of complete outage.
Budget spent is the bad events so far divided by the budget. The lab's month spent 124% of its budget; by the end of 4 June, the day of a 35-minute bad deploy, 76% was already gone.

The burn rate is the observed error ratio divided by the budget ratio, 1 − SLO: a burn rate of 1 spends the budget exactly over the window, 2 spends it in half the window, and a total outage at 99.9% burns at 1,000.
A burn rate b sustained for a time t spends b × t / window of the budget, so the whole budget lasts window / b: at 14.4, a 30-day budget lasts 50 hours, losing 2% every hour.
Background errors spend budget too: the lab's month burned at a median of 0.27 in normal hours, which on its own uses more than a quarter of the budget before any incident.

lessons.title: Error budget policies
objectives: Write an error budget policy with clear triggers and actions
Use the remaining budget to decide how much risk to take
key_points: An error budget policy, agreed in advance by the service's developers, operators and product owner, says what happens as the budget runs down, so that decisions under pressure follow a rule instead of an argument.

Typical rules: release normally while budget remains; once it's exhausted, freeze changes except reliability fixes and security patches until the service is back within its SLO; and require a postmortem when one incident spends a large share, 20% in the SRE Workbook's example policy.

Remaining budget is a currency for risk: spend it on faster releases, experiments, chaos tests and planned maintenance, and save it when it's low. Budget left over quarter after quarter suggests the SLO is stricter than needed or the team could move faster.

Say what doesn't count and who decides: an outage caused by a provider outside the team's control may be excluded or tracked separately, but name the person who rules on exclusions so that they don't become a habit.
Name who settles disagreements, such as the head of engineering, and review the policy whenever the SLO changes.

lessons.title: Alerting on burn rate
objectives: Explain why alerts on raw error-ratio thresholds page too often
Design multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts and estimate how fast they fire
key_points: Alert on what threatens the SLO, not on every blip: a rule paging whenever the 5-minute error ratio passed the SLO's 0.1% fired 648 times in the lab's month, almost all false alarms, because single errors at low traffic exceed it.
Page when the budget burns fast: 14.4 over an hour spends 2% of a 30-day budget, and 6 over 6 hours spends 5%. A slow burn, such as 1 over 3 days (10% of the budget), deserves a ticket, not a page.

A long window alone keeps firing long after a fix, so each rule also needs a short window a twelfth as long (5 minutes for 1 hour, 30 for 6 hours) showing the burn continues; in the lab, firing after recovery fell from 67 minutes to 39.

Time to detect is the long window × threshold ÷ actual burn rate: a total outage at 99.9% pages within a minute, but a burn of 15, just over 14.4, takes most of an hour, longer if noise holds it near the threshold (103 minutes in the lab).

Each SLO needs its own alerts: the availability rules never saw the lab's latency incident, which only the latency SLO's rule caught. Low-traffic services may need synthetic traffic or longer windows, since a few errors swing the ratio.
Observability with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry implements these rules in PromQL and tests them with promtool; the design decisions here carry over to any monitoring system.

"""Module 2 lab: the error budget for a 99.9% availability SLO over the 28 days, day by day."""
import pandas as pd

SLO = 0.999
df = pd.read_csv("data/traffic.csv", parse_dates=["minute"])
budget = (1 - SLO) * df.requests.sum()          # bad requests the SLO allows over the whole window
print(f"SLO {SLO:.1%} over 28 days: budget {budget:,.0f} failed requests of {df.requests.sum():,}")
print(f"as time: {(1 - SLO) * 28 * 24 * 60:.1f} minutes of complete outage")

daily = df.groupby(df.minute.dt.date)[["requests", "errors_5xx"]].sum()
daily["spent"] = daily.errors_5xx.cumsum() / budget
for day, row in daily.iterrows():
    if row.errors_5xx > 0.05 * budget or day == daily.index[-1]:
        print(f"{day}: {int(row.errors_5xx):>5} failed, {row.spent:7.1%} of the budget spent so far")
over = daily.index[daily.spent > 1]
print(f"budget exhausted on {over[0]}" if len(over) else "budget not exhausted")

hourly = df.set_index("minute")[["requests", "errors_5xx"]].resample("1h").sum()
hourly["burn"] = hourly.errors_5xx / hourly.requests / (1 - SLO)
top = hourly.burn.idxmax()
print(f"highest hourly burn rate: {hourly.burn.max():.1f} at {top:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}, which would empty a full "
      f"28-day budget in {28 * 24 / hourly.burn.max():.1f} hours")
quiet = hourly.burn[hourly.burn < 2].median()
print(f"median burn rate in normal hours: {quiet:.2f}")

"""Module 2 lab, part 2: replay the month through five alerting rules and score them against the known
incidents: how soon each one notifies, how long it keeps firing afterwards, and how many false alarms."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/traffic.csv", parse_dates=["minute"])
incidents = pd.read_csv("data/incidents.csv")
KEEP_FIRING = 10                       # minutes an alert keeps firing after its condition clears
total = df.requests.to_numpy()
slos = {"availability": (df.errors_5xx.to_numpy(), 0.999),          # bad events, SLO
        "latency": ((df.requests - df.le_300ms).to_numpy(), 0.99)}   # slower than 300 ms


def burn(sli, window):
    """Burn rate over the trailing window, evaluated every minute: error ratio / error budget."""
    bad, slo = slos[sli]
    b = pd.Series(bad).rolling(window, min_periods=1).sum().to_numpy()
    n = pd.Series(total).rolling(window, min_periods=1).sum().to_numpy()
    return b / np.maximum(n, 1) / (1 - slo)


def multiwindow(sli):
    return ((burn(sli, 60) > 14.4) & (burn(sli, 5) > 14.4)) | ((burn(sli, 360) > 6) & (burn(sli, 30) > 6))


rules = {
    "naive: 5m error ratio > 0.1%": burn("availability", 5) > 1,
    "availability, 1h burn > 14.4": burn("availability", 60) > 14.4,
    "availability, multiwindow page": multiwindow("availability"),
    "availability, ticket (3d and 6h > 1)": (burn("availability", 3 * 1440) > 1) & (burn("availability", 360) > 1),
    "latency, multiwindow page": multiwindow("latency"),
}
spans = []
for _, inc in incidents.iterrows():
    start = int((pd.Timestamp(inc.start, tz="UTC") - df.minute[0]).total_seconds() // 60)
    spans.append((inc["name"], start, start + int(inc.minutes)))


def hold(firing):
    """Keep firing for KEEP_FIRING minutes after the condition clears, as Prometheus's keep_firing_for does."""
    return pd.Series(firing.astype(int)).rolling(KEEP_FIRING + 1, min_periods=1).max().to_numpy().astype(bool)


def notifications(held):
    """Start and end minute of each continuous run of firing: one notification per run."""
    edges = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], held.astype(int), [0]]))
    return list(zip(np.flatnonzero(edges == 1), np.flatnonzero(edges == -1)))


for name, firing in rules.items():
    held = hold(firing)
    runs = notifications(held)
    print(f"{name}: {len(runs)} notifications")
    for inc, s, e in spans:
        fired = np.flatnonzero(held[s:e + 60])                      # during the incident or the hour after it
        if len(fired) == 0:
            print(f"   {inc:<24} missed")
            continue
        quiet = np.flatnonzero(~held[e:])                           # first minute after the end with no alert
        print(f"   {inc:<24} firing {fired[0]:>3} min after it began, stopped {quiet[0]:>3} min after it ended")
    false = [r for r in runs if not any(r[0] < e + 60 and r[1] > s for _, s, e in spans)]
    print(f"   false alarms: {len(false)}")

hints: Detection times are minutes from each incident's start; 'missed' means the rule didn't fire during the incident or in the hour after it.
The ticket rule's 3-day window sees less than three days of history at the start of the month, so treat its early behaviour with care.
Multiply the median burn rate by the window to see what normal operation spends: a burn of 0.27 for the whole 28 days spends 27% of the budget.

modules.title: Toil, automation and on-call
modules.summary: Measure the operational work that grows with the service and crowds out engineering, automate it safely, and design an on-call rotation that people can sustain.

lessons.title: Toil: what it is and how to measure it
objectives: Identify toil from its defining characteristics
Measure toil and decide which sources to remove first
key_points: Toil is operational work that's manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without lasting value, and that grows as the service grows: restarting a stuck worker every night is toil; designing the fix that stops it sticking is engineering.
Not all operational work is toil: handling a new kind of incident, planning capacity and writing a postmortem take judgement and leave something lasting behind.

Google's SRE teams aim to keep toil below half of each engineer's time, so that the rest goes on engineering that reduces future toil; a team past that point becomes an operations team with no capacity to improve.

Measure it: tag tickets and pages by category, record the time spent and review the totals regularly. Rank sources by hours, not by count: in the lab, 151 access requests took fewer hours than 49 manual data fixes.

Match the fix to the source: automate a repeatable procedure, offer self-service for requests, fix the bug that makes manual data repairs necessary, and tune or delete an alert that pages without needing action.

lessons.title: Automating operations safely
objectives: Design automation that is idempotent, observable and safe to run
Estimate whether automating a task pays back
key_points: Automation runs faster and more often than people, so its mistakes spread further: give operational scripts a dry run by default, a limit on how much one run may change, and an explicit opt-in for what they may touch.
Make actions idempotent: running the automation twice must leave the same result as running it once, so it can be retried after a failure or run on a schedule without checking first.
Change things atomically, for example by writing a temporary file and renaming it, so that a crash leaves either the old state or the new one, never a half-written file.
Log every action, and test the automation like any other code, including its refusals: the lab's log cleaner has tests proving it won't touch an unmarked directory or exceed its action limit.

Payback is the time to build and maintain the automation divided by the time it saves each month. Start with the largest sources, and count the mistakes and interruptions it removes, not only the minutes.

Automation grows in stages: a written runbook, a script someone runs, a script the system runs on a trigger, and finally a design that needs no procedure at all, such as log rotation built into the service.

lessons.title: Sustainable on-call
objectives: Design an on-call rotation with clear responsibilities and handovers
Measure on-call load and reduce it
key_points: On-call means being reachable and able to respond within an agreed time, typically minutes for a page. A rotation needs primary and secondary responders, an escalation path, and a handover at each change of shift that lists open issues.

Every page should need urgent human action; anything else belongs in a ticket or on a dashboard. Track pages per shift, the share at night and the share that led to action, and treat a page that needed nothing as a bug.

"""Generate four weeks of an operations team's work log: pages, tickets and project work, with the time
each took. Fixed seed, so everyone gets the same data/worklog.csv."""
import pathlib

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
team = ["ana", "ben", "chidi"]
on_call = ["ben", "chidi", "ana", "ben"]            # primary on-call, one week each from Monday 09:00
kinds = {  # category: (kind, per week, typical minutes, toil?, the fix)
    "disk full: old logs": ("page", 15, 40, "yes", "automate"),
    "restart stuck worker": ("page", 10, 25, "yes", "automate"),
    "flaky alert": ("page", 15, 10, "yes", "tune or delete the alert"),
    "certificate renewal": ("ticket", 2, 60, "yes", "automate"),
    "access request": ("ticket", 35, 12, "yes", "self-service"),
    "deploy help": ("ticket", 15, 45, "yes", "self-service"),
    "manual data fix": ("ticket", 10, 60, "yes", "fix the bug"),
    "incident response": ("page", 1, 120, "no", ""),
    "postmortem actions": ("project", 2, 180, "no", ""),
    "capacity review": ("project", 1, 120, "no", ""),
    "engineering project": ("project", 7, 300, "no", ""),
}
start = pd.Timestamp("2026-06-01 09:00", tz="UTC")
rows = []
for week in range(4):
    for category, (kind, per_week, minutes, toil, fix) in kinds.items():
        for _ in range(rng.poisson(per_week)):
            if kind == "page":   # pages arrive at any hour and go to that week's on-call engineer
                when = start + pd.Timedelta(days=7 * week) + pd.Timedelta(minutes=int(rng.integers(0, 7 * 1440)))
                who = on_call[week]
            else:                # other work happens in office hours, Monday to Friday
                when = (start + pd.Timedelta(days=7 * week + int(rng.integers(0, 5)))
                        + pd.Timedelta(minutes=int(rng.integers(0, 8 * 60))))
                who = team[int(rng.integers(0, len(team)))]
            rows.append({"time": when.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ"), "engineer": who, "kind": kind,
                         "category": category, "minutes": int(max(5, rng.normal(minutes, minutes / 4))),
                         "toil": toil, "fix": fix})
df = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("time")
pathlib.Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
df.to_csv("data/worklog.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote data/worklog.csv: {len(df)} entries over 4 weeks")

"""Module 3 lab: how much of the team's logged work is toil, where it comes from, what automating it would
pay back, and how heavy on-call is."""
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/worklog.csv", parse_dates=["time"])
hours = df.minutes.sum() / 60
toil = df[df.toil == "yes"]
print(f"logged {hours:.0f} hours of operational and project work; toil {toil.minutes.sum() / 60:.0f} hours "
      f"({toil.minutes.sum() / df.minutes.sum():.0%})")
share = (toil.groupby("engineer").minutes.sum() / df.groupby("engineer").minutes.sum()).sort_values()
print("toil share of each engineer's logged time: " + ", ".join(f"{e} {v:.0%}" for e, v in share.items()))

by = toil.groupby(["category", "fix"]).minutes.agg(["count", "sum"]).sort_values("sum", ascending=False)
by["hours per month"] = by["sum"] / 60
print(by[["count", "hours per month"]].to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"))

BUILD_HOURS = {"disk full: old logs": 16, "restart stuck worker": 24, "certificate renewal": 12}
print("automation payback (months until the build time is repaid):")
for category, build in BUILD_HOURS.items():
    monthly = toil.minutes[toil.category == category].sum() / 60
    print(f"  {category:<22} {monthly:5.1f} h/month saved, {build} h to build: {build / monthly:.1f} months")

pages = df[df.kind == "page"].copy()
pages["week"] = (pages.time - pd.Timestamp("2026-06-01 09:00", tz="UTC")).dt.days // 7 + 1
night = (pages.time.dt.hour < 8) | (pages.time.dt.hour >= 20)
print(f"pages: {len(pages)} in 4 weeks, {night.mean():.0%} between 20:00 and 08:00")
shift = pages.set_index("time").minutes.resample("12h", offset="8h").count()
print(f"pages per week: {pages.groupby('week').size().to_dict()}; busiest 12-hour shift: {shift.max()} pages "
      f"(starting {shift.idxmax():%a %d %b %H:%M})")

"""Create a sample log directory: a log per day for the last 12 days, and archives from 35-45 days ago."""
import gzip
import os
import random
import time
from pathlib import Path

random.seed(3)
root = Path("logs")
root.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(root / ".clean-logs").touch()
now = time.time()
for age in range(12):
    path = root / f"checkout-{age:02d}d.log"
    path.write_text("".join(f"{i} INFO request ok latency_ms={random.randint(5, 900)}\n" for i in range(40_000)))
    os.utime(path, (now - age * 86400 - 3600, now - age * 86400 - 3600))
for age in (35, 40, 45):
    path = root / f"checkout-{age:02d}d.log.gz"
    with gzip.open(path, "wt") as f:
        f.write("old\n" * 10_000)
    os.utime(path, (now - age * 86400, now - age * 86400))
print(f"created {len(list(root.glob('*.log')))} logs and {len(list(root.glob('*.log.gz')))} archives in logs/")

"""Compress application logs after a few days and delete old archives, safely.

Safety rails: it only touches a directory that contains a .clean-logs marker file, it does nothing unless
--apply is given, it refuses to run if more actions are planned than --max-actions, it never follows
symlinks, and every action is logged. Running it twice in a row does nothing the second time."""
import argparse
import gzip
import os
import shutil
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

MARKER = ".clean-logs"


def plan(root: Path, compress_after: float, delete_after: float, now: float):
    """Return the (action, path) pairs to perform, oldest first, without changing anything."""
    actions = []
    for path in sorted(root.iterdir()):
        if path.is_symlink() or not path.is_file():
            continue
        age_days = (now - path.stat().st_mtime) / 86400
        if path.name.endswith(".log") and age_days > compress_after:
            actions.append(("compress", path))
        elif path.name.endswith(".log.gz") and age_days > delete_after:
            actions.append(("delete", path))
    return actions


def compress(path: Path):
    """gzip to a temporary name, then rename: a crash never leaves a half-written archive."""
    tmp = path.with_name(path.name + ".gz.tmp")
    with open(path, "rb") as src, gzip.open(tmp, "wb") as dst:
        shutil.copyfileobj(src, dst)
    stat = path.stat()
    os.utime(tmp, (stat.st_atime, stat.st_mtime))       # keep the log's age on the archive
    os.replace(tmp, path.with_name(path.name + ".gz"))
    path.unlink()


def main(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    p.add_argument("root", type=Path)
    p.add_argument("--compress-after", type=float, default=3, help="days")
    p.add_argument("--delete-after", type=float, default=30, help="days")
    p.add_argument("--max-actions", type=int, default=50)
    p.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="make the changes (default: dry run)")
    a = p.parse_args(argv)

    root = a.root.resolve()
    if not (root / MARKER).is_file():
        print(f"refusing: {root} has no {MARKER} marker file", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    actions = plan(root, a.compress_after, a.delete_after, time.time())
    if len(actions) > a.max_actions:
        print(f"refusing: {len(actions)} actions planned, more than --max-actions {a.max_actions}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    freed = 0
    for action, path in actions:
        size = path.stat().st_size
        if not a.apply:
            print(f"would {action} {path.name}")
            continue
        if action == "compress":
            compress(path)
            freed += size - path.with_name(path.name + ".gz").stat().st_size
        else:
            path.unlink()
            freed += size
        print(f"{'compressed' if action == 'compress' else 'deleted'} {path.name}")
    mode = "applied" if a.apply else "dry run"
    print(f"{mode}: {sum(x == 'compress' for x, _ in actions)} to compress, "
          f"{sum(x == 'delete' for x, _ in actions)} to delete, {freed / 1e6:.1f} MB freed")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

"""Tests for clean_logs.py: run with pytest -q."""
import gzip
import os
import time

import clean_logs

DAY = 86400


def make(dir, name, age_days, text="line\n" * 1000):
    path = dir / name
    if name.endswith(".gz"):
        with gzip.open(path, "wt") as f:
            f.write(text)
    else:
        path.write_text(text)
    when = time.time() - age_days * DAY
    os.utime(path, (when, when))
    return path


def logs(tmp_path):
    (tmp_path / ".clean-logs").touch()
    make(tmp_path, "app-new.log", 1)
    make(tmp_path, "app-old.log", 5)
    make(tmp_path, "app-ancient.log.gz", 40)
    make(tmp_path, "app-recent.log.gz", 10)
    return tmp_path


def names(dir):
    return sorted(p.name for p in dir.iterdir())


def test_dry_run_changes_nothing(tmp_path):
    before = names(logs(tmp_path))
    assert clean_logs.main([str(tmp_path)]) == 0
    assert names(tmp_path) == before


def test_apply_compresses_old_logs_and_keeps_new_ones(tmp_path):
    clean_logs.main([str(logs(tmp_path)), "--apply"])
    assert "app-old.log.gz" in names(tmp_path) and "app-old.log" not in names(tmp_path)
    assert "app-new.log" in names(tmp_path)


def test_compressed_archive_holds_the_same_text(tmp_path):
    original = (logs(tmp_path) / "app-old.log").read_text()
    clean_logs.main([str(tmp_path), "--apply"])
    with gzip.open(tmp_path / "app-old.log.gz", "rt") as f:
        assert f.read() == original


def test_apply_deletes_only_expired_archives(tmp_path):
    clean_logs.main([str(logs(tmp_path)), "--apply"])
    assert "app-ancient.log.gz" not in names(tmp_path)
    assert "app-recent.log.gz" in names(tmp_path)


def test_second_run_does_nothing(tmp_path, capsys):
    clean_logs.main([str(logs(tmp_path)), "--apply"])
    after_first = names(tmp_path)
    clean_logs.main([str(tmp_path), "--apply"])
    assert names(tmp_path) == after_first
    assert "applied: 0 to compress, 0 to delete" in capsys.readouterr().out


def test_refuses_a_directory_without_the_marker(tmp_path):
    make(tmp_path, "app-old.log", 5)
    assert clean_logs.main([str(tmp_path), "--apply"]) == 2
    assert names(tmp_path) == ["app-old.log"]


def test_refuses_when_more_actions_than_the_limit(tmp_path):
    logs(tmp_path)
    for i in range(5):
        make(tmp_path, f"extra-{i}.log", 6)
    assert clean_logs.main([str(tmp_path), "--apply", "--max-actions", "3"]) == 2
    assert "extra-0.log" in names(tmp_path)

modules.title: Incident response and blameless postmortems
modules.summary: Run an incident with clear roles and steady communication, keep a timeline as you go, mitigate before you diagnose, and learn from it with a blameless postmortem.

lessons.title: Incident roles and severity
objectives: Assign the roles in an incident response and explain each
Decide when to declare an incident and how severe it is
key_points: Declare an incident early, as soon as user impact is likely or the cause isn't clear: declaring brings in roles and communication, and it's cheaper to stand down an incident than to organise a large one late.

The incident commander (IC) coordinates and decides but doesn't debug; the operations lead and responders work on the system; the communications lead keeps stakeholders informed; a scribe keeps the timeline. One person may hold several roles, but the IC is always named.
The structure borrows from the Incident Command System used by emergency services: one commander, clear roles, and one place for the response, such as a single chat channel and call.

Severity levels, such as SEV-1 to SEV-4, are defined in advance by user impact (how many users, which journeys, whether data is at risk), and set who is paged, how often updates go out and whether a postmortem is required.
Hand over explicitly: when the IC or the operations lead changes, say so in the channel, with a summary of the current state, so that nobody wonders who's in charge.
Security incidents follow the same discipline plus evidence handling and legal duties, which Incident Response Fundamentals covers.

lessons.title: Mitigation, communication and the timeline
objectives: Put mitigation before root cause during an incident
Write status updates and keep a timeline in UTC
key_points: Mitigate first: roll back the last change, fail over, shed load or switch off a feature to stop the user impact, and find the root cause afterwards. In the lab's incident, rolling back a configuration change ended it minutes after the decision.
Ask what changed: many incidents follow a deployment, a configuration change or a shift in traffic, so the deploy and change logs belong in the timeline and are among the first places to look.

Send status updates on a stated cadence, every 30 minutes for example, even when there's no news: what's affected, what's being done, any workaround and when the next update comes. Internal and external audiences need different detail.

Keep the timeline as you go, in UTC: alerts, decisions, actions and observations with their times. Systems log in different time zones and formats, so normalise them before merging, as the lab's script does.

Measure each response from its timeline: time to detect (impact to alert), to mitigate and to recover. Averages over a few incidents are noisy because durations vary widely, so read each incident's story rather than tracking a mean.

lessons.title: Blameless postmortems
objectives: Write a blameless postmortem with contributing factors and action items
Decide when a postmortem is required and how to follow it up
key_points: Write a postmortem after significant incidents, defined in advance: user-visible downtime or data loss beyond a threshold, any on-call intervention such as a rollback, or a large share of the error budget spent in one incident.

Blameless means assuming people acted reasonably with the information and tools they had: ask why the system allowed the mistake and made it hard to catch, not who made it. People who fear blame hide the details that would prevent the next incident.

Avoid 'human error' and single root causes: list the contributing factors, such as a risky change without review, a missing safety limit, an alert that pointed elsewhere, and a slow route to the change log, each with its own fix.

A postmortem covers the summary, impact in numbers, detection, response, the timeline, contributing factors, what went well and badly, where the team got lucky, and action items with owners, priorities and tickets.
Action items only matter once they're done: make them specific and tracked, review them regularly, and share postmortems widely so that other teams learn from them too.

"""Write incident/metrics.csv: checkout's per-minute requests and 5xx errors from 13:30 to 15:30 UTC."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
minutes = pd.date_range("2026-07-09 13:30", "2026-07-09 15:29", freq="min", tz="UTC")
requests = rng.poisson(310, len(minutes))
t = (minutes - pd.Timestamp("2026-07-09 14:02:11", tz="UTC")).total_seconds() / 60
ratio = np.where((t > 2) & (minutes < pd.Timestamp("2026-07-09 14:39", tz="UTC")),
                 np.minimum(0.35, 0.05 * (t - 2)), 0.0003)          # the pool drains, errors climb to 35%
ratio = np.where((minutes >= pd.Timestamp("2026-07-09 14:39", tz="UTC")) &
                 (minutes < pd.Timestamp("2026-07-09 14:42", tz="UTC")), 0.05, ratio)   # draining after rollback
errors = rng.binomial(requests, ratio)
pd.DataFrame({"minute": minutes.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ"), "requests": requests, "errors_5xx": errors}).to_csv(
    "incident/metrics.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote incident/metrics.csv: {len(minutes)} minutes")

"""Module 4 lab: merge the incident's deploy log, alerts, chat and metrics into one UTC timeline, and
measure detection, mitigation and recovery, and the error budget the incident spent."""
import json
import re
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import pandas as pd

events = []
for line in open("incident/deploys.log"):                     # local time with an offset: convert to UTC
    stamp, text = line[:25], line[26:].strip()
    events.append((datetime.strptime(stamp, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z").astimezone(timezone.utc), "deploy", text))
for alert in json.load(open("incident/alerts.json")):          # ISO 8601 in UTC
    key = "startsAt" if alert["status"] == "firing" else "endsAt"
    when = datetime.fromisoformat(alert[key].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    events.append((when, "alert", f"{alert['labels']['alertname']} {alert['status']}"))
for line in open("incident/chat.txt"):                         # [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC] who: text
    m = re.match(r"\[(.+?) UTC\] (.+)", line.strip())
    events.append((datetime.strptime(m[1], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M").replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc), "chat", m[2]))

m = pd.read_csv("incident/metrics.csv", parse_dates=["minute"])
m["ratio"] = m.errors_5xx / m.requests
bad = m[m.ratio > 0.01]
impact_start, impact_end = bad.minute.min().to_pydatetime(), bad.minute.max().to_pydatetime()
ratio10 = m.errors_5xx.rolling(10).sum() / m.requests.rolling(10).sum()     # trailing 10 minutes
calm = (ratio10 < 0.001) & (m.minute - pd.Timedelta(minutes=9) > bad.minute.max())
recovered = m.minute[calm].min().to_pydatetime() - pd.Timedelta(minutes=9)  # start of the first calm 10 minutes
events += [(impact_start, "metrics", "error ratio above 1%: impact begins"),
           (impact_end, "metrics", "last minute with error ratio above 1%"),
           (recovered, "metrics", "recovered: the 10 minutes from here have an error ratio under 0.1%")]

events.sort(key=lambda e: e[0])
lo, hi = impact_start - pd.Timedelta(minutes=30), recovered + pd.Timedelta(minutes=30)
for when, source, text in events:
    if lo <= when <= hi:
        print(f"{when:%H:%M:%S}  {source:<7} {text}")


def first(source, pattern):
    return next(w for w, s, t in events if s == source and re.search(pattern, t))


change = first("deploy", "CHG-4471")
page = first("alert", "firing")
rollback = first("deploy", "rollback-of=CHG-4471")
minutes = lambda a, b: (b - a).total_seconds() / 60
print(f"trigger to impact: {minutes(change, impact_start):.1f} min; impact to page (time to detect): "
      f"{minutes(impact_start, page):.1f} min")
print(f"impact to rollback (time to mitigate): {minutes(impact_start, rollback):.1f} min; impact to recovery: "
      f"{minutes(impact_start, recovered):.1f} min")
window = m[(m.minute >= impact_start) & (m.minute < recovered)]
failed = int(window.errors_5xx.sum())
BUDGET = 0.001 * 6_282_951                  # 99.9% of 28 days at the traffic level of module 1
print(f"failed requests during the incident: {failed:,} = {failed / BUDGET:.0%} of the 28-day error budget")

# Postmortem: <short title of what users experienced>

Status: draft | in review | final
Incident: SEV-<n>, <date>, <start>-<end> UTC
Authors: <names>    Reviewers: <names>

## Summary
Two or three sentences: what users experienced, for how long, the trigger, and how it was mitigated.

## Impact
Who was affected and how: failed or slow requests, users or orders affected, revenue or data at risk,
and the error budget spent (% of the 28-day budget). Use numbers from the metrics, not impressions.

## Detection
How we found out (alert, customer, colleague), and how long after impact began.
Did the right alert fire? Would it have fired at 3 am at half the traffic?

## Response and recovery
What was done, by whom (roles, not blame), and what mitigated it. What slowed us down?

## Timeline (UTC)
| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| hh:mm | ... |

modules.summary: Plan capacity with headroom and queueing in mind, release changes gradually with automated canary analysis, and test resilience with careful chaos experiments.

lessons.title: Capacity planning
objectives: Forecast demand and size a service with headroom and redundancy
Explain why latency rises sharply as utilisation approaches 100%
key_points: Capacity planning forecasts organic demand from trend and seasonality, adds inorganic demand such as launches and marketing events, and turns the forecast peak into resources using a measured capacity per instance.
Measure capacity per instance with a load test: the throughput at which latency still meets the SLO, below the knee where queues build, not the most it can survive.

Little's law, L = λW, says the average number of requests in a system is the arrival rate times the time each spends there: 600 requests per second each holding a worker for 50 ms keep 30 workers busy on average.

Queueing delay climbs steeply near saturation: in an M/M/c model carrying 30 workers' worth of load, 32 workers (94% busy) give an average wait of about 16 ms and 40 workers (75%) under 1 ms, so plan for headroom, not for 100%.

Provision for failure too: N+1 or N+2 means the peak is still served with one or two instances, or a whole zone, lost; across three zones, each must carry half the peak if one fails. Allow for capacity that takes weeks to arrive.

lessons.title: Release engineering and progressive delivery
objectives: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary releases and feature flags
Gate a canary on its SLIs with an automated comparison
key_points: Release engineering makes change repeatable and reversible: builds reproducible from source, versioned artefacts, configuration treated as code, and a rollback that is tested and fast, since many incidents start with a change.

A rolling update replaces instances a few at a time; blue-green runs the new version beside the old and switches all traffic at once, with an instant way back; a canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first, widening it in steps while comparing SLIs.

Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature: ship it switched off, turn it on for some users, and turn it off in seconds if it misbehaves. Remove each flag once its feature is fully released.

Compare a canary with a baseline of the same size started at the same time, not with the long-running fleet, so that warm caches and uptime don't bias the result, and judge it on SLIs with a statistical test and a minimum effect size, as the lab does.

Small canaries need time: detecting an error ratio rising from 0.03% to 0.06% takes about 100,000 requests per group (80% power, one-sided 1% significance), about 33 minutes at 50 requests per second but over 5 hours at 5.

Progressive delivery tools, such as Argo Rollouts and Flagger on Kubernetes, automate the steps: shift traffic, query the metrics, then promote or roll back. Configuration changes deserve the same care as code: the module 4 incident was a configuration change pushed everywhere at once.

lessons.title: Chaos engineering basics
objectives: Design a chaos experiment with a steady-state hypothesis and abort conditions
Decide where and how to start practising chaos engineering
key_points: Chaos engineering tests resilience by experiment: state a steady-state hypothesis as an SLI, such as '99% of product pages succeed within 500 ms', inject a realistic fault, and look for a difference from normal behaviour.

Choose faults that happen in real life: an instance or zone lost, a dependency slow or failing, a full disk, clock skew, a network partition. Netflix's Chaos Monkey, which shuts down instances at random, made the practice widely known.

Limit the blast radius: start in a test environment, then a small share of production traffic, with abort conditions that stop the experiment and remove the fault automatically when the SLI falls below a floor.

Experiments find weaknesses before users do: in the lab, a shop with a 200 ms timeout and a fallback kept every page good while its recommender failed or slowed; without them, a quarter to a third of pages failed, and a 2-second slowdown broke them all.
Run game days, planned exercises in which a team practises a failure and its response together, and spend error budget deliberately on experiments; fix what they reveal before widening their scope.

"""Module 5 lab: judge three canary releases automatically. Each canary is compared with a baseline of the
same size started at the same time, on errors (5xx) and on slow requests (over 300 ms)."""
import math

RUNS = {  # release: {group: (requests, 5xx errors, slower than 300 ms)}, over a 60-minute analysis window
    "v2.3.1": {"baseline": (48_210, 14, 362), "canary": (47_985, 17, 371)},
    "v2.4.0": {"baseline": (49_020, 15, 377), "canary": (48_870, 61, 402)},
    "v2.5.0": {"baseline": (48_640, 13, 355), "canary": (48_515, 16, 698)},
}
ALPHA, MIN_RATIO = 0.01, 1.2      # fail only if significantly worse AND at least 20% worse


def one_sided_p(bad_c, n_c, bad_b, n_b):
    """Two-proportion z-test: how likely is a canary this much worse if it were really no worse?"""
    pooled = (bad_c + bad_b) / (n_c + n_b)
    se = math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n_c + 1 / n_b))
    z = (bad_c / n_c - bad_b / n_b) / se if se else 0.0
    return z, 0.5 * math.erfc(z / math.sqrt(2))


for release, run in RUNS.items():
    (n_b, err_b, slow_b), (n_c, err_c, slow_c) = run["baseline"], run["canary"]
    failed = []
    for sli, bc, bb in (("errors", err_c, err_b), ("slow", slow_c, slow_b)):
        z, p = one_sided_p(bc, n_c, bb, n_b)
        worse = (bc / n_c) / (bb / n_b)
        if p < ALPHA and worse > MIN_RATIO:
            failed.append(sli)
        print(f"{release} {sli:<6} canary {bc / n_c:.3%} vs baseline {bb / n_b:.3%}  ({worse:.2f}x, z={z:5.2f}, "
              f"p={p:.4f})")
    print(f"{release}: {'ROLL BACK (' + ', '.join(failed) + ')' if failed else 'PROMOTE'}")

# How long must a canary run to catch a doubling of a 0.03% error ratio (power 80%, one-sided alpha 0.01)?
p1, p2 = 0.0003, 0.0006
z_a, z_b = 2.326, 0.842
n = ((z_a * math.sqrt(2 * (p1 + p2) / 2 * (1 - (p1 + p2) / 2)) + z_b * math.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2)))
     / (p2 - p1)) ** 2
for rps in (5, 50):
    print(f"to detect 0.03% -> 0.06%: {n:,.0f} requests per group, {n / rps / 60:,.0f} minutes at {rps} requests/s")

"""The shop's product page. It calls the recommender with a short timeout and, when FALLBACK=on, shows
bestsellers instead if the recommender is slow or failing."""
import os

import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()
RECOMMENDER = os.environ.get("RECOMMENDER_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8101")
GUARDED = os.environ.get("FALLBACK", "on") == "on"
client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=0.2 if GUARDED else 30.0)    # 200 ms budget for the dependency
BESTSELLERS = [1, 2, 3]


@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"status": "ok", "fallback": GUARDED}


@app.get("/product/{product_id}")
async def product(product_id: int, user: int = 0):
    try:
        r = await client.get(f"{RECOMMENDER}/recommendations/{user}")
        r.raise_for_status()
        items, source = r.json()["items"], "recommender"
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        if not GUARDED:                 # unguarded: the dependency's failure becomes ours
            raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="recommendations unavailable")
        items, source = BESTSELLERS, "fallback"
    return {"product": product_id, "recommended": items, "source": source}

"""Module 5 lab, part 2: a chaos experiment on your own machine. Steady-state hypothesis: at least 99% of
product pages return 200 within 500 ms, even when the recommender fails or slows down."""
import asyncio
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import httpx

SHOP, RECOMMENDER = "http://127.0.0.1:8100", "http://127.0.0.1:8101"
TARGET, ABORT = 0.99, 0.50          # the hypothesis, and the level at which we stop injecting at once


def start(module, port, **env):
    cmd = [sys.executable, "-m", "uvicorn", f"{module}:app", "--port", str(port), "--log-level", "error"]
    proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, env={**os.environ, **env})
    for _ in range(100):
        try:
            httpx.get(f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/health", timeout=0.5)
            return proc
        except httpx.HTTPError:
            time.sleep(0.1)
    proc.terminate()
    raise SystemExit(f"{module} didn't start on port {port}")


async def measure(n=200, concurrency=20):
    """Send n product-page requests; return the share that were good and the share served by the fallback."""
    good = fallback = 0
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as c:
        async def one(i):
            nonlocal good, fallback
            async with sem:
                t0 = time.perf_counter()
                try:
                    r = await c.get(f"{SHOP}/product/{i % 50}", params={"user": i})
                    ok = r.status_code == 200 and time.perf_counter() - t0 < 0.5
                    fallback += r.status_code == 200 and r.json()["source"] == "fallback"
                except httpx.HTTPError:
                    ok = False
                good += ok
        await asyncio.gather(*(one(i) for i in range(n)))
    return good / n, fallback / n


def inject(latency_ms=0, error_rate=0.0):
    httpx.post(f"{RECOMMENDER}/chaos", params={"latency_ms": latency_ms, "error_rate": error_rate})


recommender = start("recommender", 8101)
try:
    for guard in ("on", "off"):
        shop = start("shop", 8100, FALLBACK=guard)
        try:
            for phase, latency, errors in [("steady state", 0, 0.0), ("30% of calls fail", 0, 0.3),
                                           ("calls 2 s slower", 2000, 0.0)]:
                inject(latency, errors)
                good, fallback = asyncio.run(measure())
                inject()                                        # roll the fault back straight away
                verdict = "hypothesis holds" if good >= TARGET else "hypothesis broken"
                print(f"fallback {guard:<3} | {phase:<17} | good {good:6.1%} | fallback used {fallback:6.1%} | {verdict}")
                if good < ABORT:
                    print(f"fallback {guard:<3} | abort: good requests fell below {ABORT:.0%}; fault removed, "
                          f"experiment stopped")
                    break
        finally:
            shop.terminate()
            shop.wait()
finally:
    recommender.terminate()
    recommender.wait()

hints: If experiment.py says a service didn't start, another program is using port 8100 or 8101: stop it, or change the ports in experiment.py and set RECOMMENDER_URL for the shop.

The share of good pages in the unguarded '30% of calls fail' phase varies between runs (63.5% and 76.0% in testing), because the recommender's random failures depend on how requests interleave; the conclusion doesn't change.
At 150 ms the recommender answers inside the timeout, so pages stay good only while 150 ms plus the shop's own work stays under 500 ms; on a busy laptop, try a few runs.

project.title: Define, defend and test the reliability of a service
project.brief: Take a service you run, or the course's checkout, shop and recommender services, and make its reliability explicit and defended. Define two or three SLIs for its main user journeys with exact definitions of good and valid events, set SLOs with a window and a rationale, and work out the error budgets. Write an error budget policy the product owner could sign. Design multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts for each SLO and replay at least four weeks of real or generated data through them to show their detection times and false alarms. Measure toil for at least two weeks (or use the course's work log), automate one source with a safe, tested script, and set out the on-call rotation and paging policy. Finally, run a chaos experiment with a stated hypothesis and abort conditions, fix what it reveals, and write a blameless postmortem for the failure it found or for a game day you ran.
deliverables: An SLO document: SLIs with exact definitions and where they're measured, targets, windows, error budgets, rationale, owner and review date
An error budget policy with its triggers, actions, exclusions and who decides
The alerting rules, in any monitoring system's syntax or as code, and a replay report giving detection times, time firing after recovery and false alarms for each rule
A toil report and the automation you built, with its tests and its measured or estimated payback, plus the on-call rotation and paging policy
